New managers often think the first month is about proving they deserved the promotion. That pressure usually creates the opposite result: too much explaining, too many promises, delayed feedback, and work pulled back after delegation.

A steadier first month is simpler: observe before changing, make decisions clearly, give narrow feedback early, define the finish line when delegating, and protect enough capacity to actually manage.

The First 30 Days as a New Manager is a practical manual for that transition — authority, feedback, delegation, managing up, pushback, and decision timing without motivational hype.

https://plainact-crypto.github.io/plain-act/books/the-first-30-days-as-a-new-manager/

A common new-manager mistake is not failing to delegate. It is delegating vaguely, getting nervous, then taking the work back.

A cleaner handoff has four parts: the outcome, the constraints, the checkpoint, and the finish line. Once those are clear, hovering becomes less necessary.

That is the kind of management problem Plain Act is built around: small pressure moments where the wrong reaction quietly becomes a team pattern.

The First 30 Days as a New Manager: https://plainact-crypto.github.io/plain-act/books/the-first-30-days-as-a-new-manager/

Delayed feedback gets heavier every day it waits. New managers often postpone it because they want to be fair, avoid tension, or find the perfect wording. The result is usually a bigger conversation than the original issue required.

Useful feedback is narrower: what happened, why it matters, and what needs to change next.

Plain Act focuses on management under pressure — not louder leadership language.

Read the flagship manual: https://plainact-crypto.github.io/plain-act/books/the-first-30-days-as-a-new-manager/
